summary: The note examines how legislation protects architectural heritage after September 2023, covering the amended National Heritage Preservation Act, local heritage committees, tax incentives, public education and enforcement and funding challenges. It quotes officials and experts on balancing development with conservation. It concludes that legislators, local authorities and heritage professionals must work together and sustain vigilant stewardship.
one_line: Overview of post-2023 heritage preservation law, local committees, incentives, education campaigns, enforcement and funding for protecting historic buildings.
key_facts: In October 2023 the National Heritage Preservation Act (NHPA) was amended to introduce stricter penalties for unauthorized alteration or demolition of registered historical structures.
Senator Elaine Mercer spearheaded the NHPA amendment, aimed at deterring loss of historic buildings to developers operating without proper clearances.
The NHPA amendment mandated local heritage committees of experts and community representatives to oversee preservation standards.
Mayor Franklin D'Souza of Hilltown, known for its Victorian-era boroughs, said local heritage committees give a voice to the citizens most invested in the area's history.

The State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) was established on January 18, 2024 and works with local committees to decide which buildings become heritage sites and what interventions are permissible.
Tax credits for restoring and rehabilitating heritage buildings were introduced by the government in February 2024 to encourage private investment.

Professor Lydia Zhang, an urban development expert, said well-crafted policies can facilitate adaptive reuse of historic structures, countering the misconception that preservation is anti-development.
The "History Lives Here" campaign, launched in May 2024 and directed by Dr. Alicia Reynolds, includes workshops, school programs and interactive digital platforms.
District Attorney Josephine Hart has prosecuted several heritage law violations and says stricter monitoring and heavier fines serve as a deterrent despite limited resources.
The "Heritage Revival Fund", a public-private partnership established on August 15, 2025, helps community groups raise capital for preservation projects.
Government grants do not always cover the full cost of expensive restoration projects, leaving a funding gap.
